ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A quarter-circle screen with radius $R = 0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ is placed in a uniform electric field with the electric field strength directed vertically downward, and OB is horizontal. A particle with mass $m = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and charge $q = 8.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C}$ is horizontally ejected from point A, which is at the same height as the center O of the circle and $0.3\,\mathrm{m}$ away from O, with an initial velocity $\mathbf{v}_0 = 3\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The gravitational force on the particle is negligible, and the particle just hits point C on the curved surface of the quarter-circle perpendicularly (not shown in the figure). The potential at point C is taken as $\varphi = 0$.

1. What is the magnitude $E$ of the electric field strength in this uniform electric field?
2. What is the magnitude of the velocity $v_C$ of the particle when it reaches point C?
3. What is the electric potential energy $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{p}}$ when the particle's speed is $4\mathrm{m/s}$?

The gravitational force on the particle is negligible, and the particle just hits point C on the curved surface of the quarter-circle perpendicularly. The potential at point C is taken as $\varphi = 0$. 1. What is the magnitude $E$ of the electric field strength in this uniform electric field? 2. ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are multiple vertically downward electric field lines, indicating that the direction of the uniform electric field is downward; point O is located on the upper dashed horizontal line, and OB is a horizontal dashed segment from O to the right; point A is to the left of O and at the same height as O, and the particle is launched from A horizontally to the right, with the initial velocity labeled v0; on the right is a quarter circular arc screen with O as the center, and the particle finally hits point C on the arc and is perpendicular to the arc. Reasoning: Take O as the origin, the x-axis to the right along OB, and the y-axis vertically downward. According to the problem, A=(-0.3,0), and the arc satisfies x^2+y^2=R^2=0.5^2. The particle is positively charged, gravity is ignored, and the electric field is downward, so the acceleration a=qE/m is downward. The equations of motion are x=-0.3+v0 t=-0.3+3t, y=(1/2)at^2. The particle strikes the arc perpendicularly, indicating that the velocity direction at impact is along the radius OC, so the velocity (v0,at) is parallel to the radius (x,y), that is, at/v0=y/x. Substituting y=(1/2)at^2 gives at/3=((1/2)at^2)/x, so x=1.5t. Also x=-0.3+3t, therefore -0.3+3t=1.5t, solving gives t=0.2 s. At this time x=-0.3+3×0.2=0.3 m. From the circle equation x^2+y^2=0.25, y=sqrt(0.25-0.09)=0.4 m. Then from y=(1/2)at^2, 0.4=0.5a×0.2^2=0.02a, so a=20 m/s^2. Thus E=ma/q=(10^-4×20)/(8.0×10^-5)=25 N/C. When reaching C, the vertical component of velocity vy=at=20×0.2=4 m/s, and the horizontal component of velocity vx=3 m/s, so vC=sqrt(3^2+4^2)=5 m/s. Take the electric potential at point C as 0, then the electric potential energy at point C is UC=0. Mechanical energy is conserved: K+U=KC+UC=KC. When the particle's speed is 4 m/s, the electric potential energy U=KC-K4=(1/2)m(vC^2-4^2)=0.5×10^-4×(25-16)=4.5×10^-4 J.
